rw: Bonds and cash supply steadier income and protect principal near retirement, while a smaller share of stocks still gives some growth to offset inflation over the retirement years.

ww.All money in speculative penny stocks fo: Speculative penny stocks are extremely volatile, and a retiree three years from needing income cannot afford large swings or permanent losses on an all-in bet like this.
ww.All money in one start-up expected to gr: A single start-up is a concentrated, high-failure bet, and a person three years from retirement who needs stable income has no time to recover from losing it.
ww.All money in a fund of new tech firms wi: A fund of unprofitable new tech firms is highly volatile and pays little income, so it clashes with a short horizon and a need for stable income.

rw: With forty years to invest, a diversified mix with a large stock share can ride out downturns and capture long-term growth, which suits the long horizon well.

ww.Putting everything into one stock a frie: One stock leaves the investor exposed to that company's failure, and a friend's tip is not research, so this ignores diversification even though forty years is a long horizon.
ww.Keeping all savings in a checking accoun: A checking account pays almost nothing, so inflation over forty years would steadily erode the buying power of the savings, which defeats the purpose of retirement investing.
ww.Waiting until age 60 to begin investing: Waiting until sixty throws away decades of compounding, so the investor would need to save far more later to reach the same retirement goal.

rw: Safe savings protect against sharp losses while diversified long-term investments have historically outpaced inflation, so combining them addresses both risks the question names, loss and inflation.

ww.All money placed in one risky stock the: One risky stock concentrates all the loss risk in a single company and offers no protection, so it fails to guard savings against loss over many years.
ww.All money held in cash at home where it: Cash kept at home earns no interest, so inflation steadily cuts its buying power, and it is also exposed to theft, fire, and loss.
ww.All money lent to a friend who promised: A personal loan to a friend relies on one borrower's promise, can go unpaid, and earns no reliable return, so it protects against neither loss nor inflation.

rw: A CD locks in a fixed rate for a set term, and that commitment usually earns a higher rate than a regular savings account, if the cash is not needed soon.

ww.CDs can be traded on a stock exchange at: CDs are not traded on exchanges at daily rising prices, and no investment can guarantee a price that rises every day, so this claim is false.
ww.CDs are not insured so they pay a higher: CDs issued by banks are typically insured, up to limits, by the FDIC; a higher rate comes from locking money for a term, not from lacking insurance.
ww.CDs allow unlimited withdrawals at any t: CDs normally charge a penalty for early withdrawal, so unlimited penalty-free access is false, and they do not always pay the most of every option.

rw: Tax-advantaged accounts may allow contributions to be deducted or earnings to grow tax deferred or tax free, which lowers or delays the saver's tax bill.

ww.They let the saver withdraw money at any: Early withdrawals from retirement accounts usually trigger taxes and often a penalty, so claiming access at any age with no tax or penalty is false.
ww.They guarantee that the investments will: Tax advantages concern taxes, not investment results; the account holdings can still lose value, and no retirement account guarantees that investments will never lose value.
ww.They remove the need to pay any income t: Wages are still subject to income tax; at most, contributions to some accounts are deducted, so the claim that no income tax is owed on wages is false.

rw: When most holdings sit in one industry, a downturn there can hit every position together, so diversifying across industries reduces that shared risk.

ww.All stocks in one industry must rise tog: Stocks in one industry do not all rise together, and even if they did they could all fall together, so the claim that none can fall is wrong.
ww.Investors in one industry must pay a spe: Tax law does not add a special extra tax for investing in one industry, so concentration risk comes from shared exposure, not from any levy.
ww.The law forbids investors from selling s: No law forbids selling shares in a particular industry; investors can sell freely, so the risk of concentration is about shared losses and not a legal restriction.

rw: Over thirty years, rising prices mean each dollar buys less, so savings held only in cash lose purchasing power even though the balance never falls.

ww.Cash loses all of its value on deposit: Cash deposits keep their face value, and the owner can still withdraw the full sum; the problem is lost buying power, not a loss of the deposit itself.
ww.Cash is taxed more than other assets: Cash is not generally taxed more than other assets; interest is taxed like other income, and the real long-run drawback is inflation, not tax rates.
ww.Cash can be spent only on cheap goods: Cash can buy goods of any price, cheap or expensive, so the claim that it can be spent only on cheap goods is false.

rw: Choosing only the safest assets means accepting lower returns, which gives up the higher long-term growth that riskier assets such as stocks have historically offered.

ww.The ability to earn any interest at all: Very safe assets such as insured savings and Treasury bills do pay interest, so an investor in them still earns some, only at lower rates.
ww.The right to sell holdings at will: Safe assets such as Treasury bills and savings accounts can usually be sold or withdrawn when wanted, so the investor keeps the right to sell at will.
ww.Federal government protection from loss: Many safe assets, such as insured deposits, actually carry government protection, so this is something the investor gains and not gives up by choosing safe assets.

rw: Spreading money across many holdings means one poor performer is only a small part of the portfolio, so its damage is limited, which is the point of diversification.

ww.It means owning only one stock so the in: Owning one stock is the opposite of diversification, since following one company closely does not remove the risk that it fails and takes the whole portfolio down.
ww.It guarantees that the investor will nev: Diversification lowers risk but cannot guarantee against loss, because broad market declines hit most holdings at once, so the claim of never losing money is false.
ww.It means buying every stock in the marke: Diversification does not require owning every stock in equal amounts; a handful of varied holdings can be enough, so this describes an impractical and unnecessary extreme.

rw: A strong past year says little about next year, because returns change with markets and conditions, so past performance does not guarantee that a fund will repeat it.

ww.The fund is insured against any loss by: Regulators do not insure funds against investment losses; only bank deposits or brokerage failures have limited protection, so an investment fund can still lose money.
ww.The fund will certainly repeat the same: No fund can be certain to repeat its top return, since markets shift and leaders often fall back, so assuming it will repeat is a common mistake.
ww.Fees are not important when a fund has h: Fees reduce the investor's returns every year whether or not the fund performed well, so they stay important even after a strong year.

rw: With an emergency fund in place, paying off high-interest debt gives a sure return equal to the rate saved, and investing builds wealth for long-term goals.

ww.Lend it to an acquaintance who has promi: Lending a windfall to an acquaintance is an unsecured risk that may never be repaid, and it does nothing to build the investor's own financial security.
ww.Hide it in a drawer at home for use in t: Cash hidden in a drawer earns no interest and loses buying power to inflation, and it can be stolen or lost, so it does not put the windfall to good use.
ww.Spend it all on impulse purchases within: Spending it all on impulse buys leaves nothing behind for lasting goals, and the money is gone within weeks with no lasting benefit.

rw: Starting early gives investments more years to compound, meaning earnings themselves earn returns, so a given contribution can grow much larger by retirement.

ww.Taxes disappear for all early investors: Taxes do not disappear for early investors; gains and income are taxed under the same rules, though tax-advantaged accounts can defer or reduce them.
ww.Early investors are guaranteed higher re: No return is guaranteed to anyone, early or late, so beginning early improves the odds through time and compounding but cannot promise higher returns.
ww.Early investors never pay any fees on fu: Funds charge expense ratios and sometimes sales fees whatever the investor's age or start date, so beginning early does not remove fund fees.

rw: Historically, stock returns have been negative far less often over long holding periods than short ones, because gains and losses average out and the market tends to trend upward.

ww.Stocks can be held for only ten years be: No law forces an investor to sell stocks after ten years; investors can hold shares as long as they like, so this restriction does not exist.
ww.Holding period has no effect on the risk: The holding period does matter, since short periods show wide swings and long ones smooth them out, so the chance of loss tends to fall with time.
ww.Over longer periods stocks always lose v: Stocks do not always lose value over long periods; history shows long-run gains in diversified portfolios, and risks do not simply build up until losses are certain.

rw: A goal-based approach ties each goal's time horizon and risk tolerance to suitable assets, for example safe assets for near-term needs and stocks for distant ones.

ww.Pick whichever investment is advertised: Advertising frequency says nothing about whether an investment suits a person's goals or risk, so choosing by what appears on television is not goal based.
ww.Put all money into whichever asset had t: Last period's top performer is no guide to future returns and may carry heavy risk, so chasing the highest past return ignores the goal's time horizon.
ww.Choose the investment with the lowest fe: Low fees matter, but picking the cheapest option while ignoring its risk can leave the investor with assets that do not suit the goal or timeline.

rw: A short horizon leaves no time to wait out a decline, so a price drop could force a sale at a loss just when the money is needed.

ww.The law forbids investors from selling a: No law forbids selling stocks; investors can sell on any trading day, so this is false, and the real risk to short-term money is price drops.
ww.Stock markets close for a year if money: Stock markets do not close for a year because money is held briefly; they open each business day, so this invented rule has no connection to the actual risk.
ww.Stocks always rise within six months so: Stocks can fall at any time, including within six months, so the claim that they always rise over that span is false and risk clearly exists.

rw: Speculative investments chase large profits and accept a real chance of heavy losses, so a high-risk, high-potential profile is their defining trait.

ww.Low volatility and steady income paid ev: Low volatility and steady monthly income describe conservative investments such as high-grade bonds or dividend payers, which is the opposite of speculation, with its swings.
ww.Required safety checks by the regulator: Speculative investments usually lack special safety checks; regulators require disclosure for securities, but they do not vet them for safety or soundness before sale.
ww.A guaranteed fixed return insured by the: Guaranteed insured returns describe things like bank deposits, whereas speculative investments offer no guarantee and no government insurance against loss.

rw: FINRA is the self-regulatory organization that writes and enforces rules for broker-dealers and their registered representatives, under SEC oversight, so it is the correct answer.

ww.FDIC: The FDIC insures bank deposits; it does not regulate broker-dealers or registered representatives, so it is not the self-regulatory body described in the question.
ww.The Fed: The Federal Reserve sets monetary policy and supervises banks; it is a government central bank, not a self-regulatory body for brokers and their representatives.
ww.The IRS: The IRS collects federal taxes and is a government agency, not a self-regulatory organization, and it has no role in regulating broker conduct.

rw: FINRA BrokerCheck and the SEC adviser database list registration, licenses, and disciplinary history, which makes them the official way to verify a professional.

ww.Read the ads the broker placed in the lo: Newspaper ads are marketing chosen by the broker and show nothing about registration status, so reading them cannot confirm that a broker is registered.
ww.Count the social media followers the bro: Social media followers measure popularity, not registration or good conduct, and unregistered people can attract large followings, so a follower count proves nothing.
ww.Ask the broker's friends if the person s: Friends' opinions of someone's honesty are subjective and unverifiable; they cannot show registration status or any record of complaints or sanctions.

rw: A 12b-1 fee is charged each year from fund assets to pay for marketing, distribution, and sometimes shareholder services, and it is part of the fund's expense ratio.

ww.A commission that a broker pays to the f: A 12b-1 fee is charged to the fund's shareholders from fund assets, not paid by a broker to the fund for each customer, so the direction is reversed.
ww.A tax paid on gains from selling fund sh: Taxes on gains from selling shares are capital gains taxes paid to the government; a 12b-1 fee is a fund expense, not a tax on gains.
ww.A one-time fee that the SEC charges to b: A 12b-1 fee is not a one-time charge from the SEC; it is recurring, paid by the fund itself, and it is not billed to buyers by the SEC.

rw: A transfer agent keeps the official records of who owns a company's stocks and bonds, and it handles ownership changes, so it is the record keeper for securities.

ww.A government official who approves the s: Government officials do not approve share sales as transfer agents; the SEC reviews registrations, whereas a transfer agent is a private firm that keeps ownership records.
ww.A trader who buys and sells shares on th: A trader who deals on the exchange floor for his own account is a floor trader or specialist, not a transfer agent, who keeps records.
ww.A person who moves employees from one de: Moving employees between departments is a human resources task within a firm and has nothing to do with securities, where a transfer agent tracks owners.

rw: Investment bankers advise companies and underwrite new stock or bond issues, which helps those companies raise capital from investors, and that is their core function.

ww.Collects the income taxes owed by firms: Collecting income taxes is the job of tax authorities such as the IRS, not an investment banker, whose business is advising on and underwriting securities issues.
ww.Holds ordinary customers' deposits and l: Accepting deposits and making home loans describes a commercial or retail bank; an investment banker deals with capital markets, not with ordinary customers' deposits.
ww.Insures investors against losses from st: Insuring investors against stock price falls is not what investment bankers do; insurance companies provide cover, and no one insures investors against ordinary market declines.

rw: A prime broker bundles services such as securities lending, margin financing, and trade clearing for large clients like hedge funds, which matches this description.

ww.A broker who works free of charge for ch: Prime brokers are commercial firms serving institutional clients and charge fees, so working free for charities is not what defines them, and the description is incorrect.
ww.A government official who is in charge o: A prime broker is a private firm and not a government official, and exchanges are run by their own management, not by a prime broker.
ww.A broker who sells only the highest qual: A prime broker serves large clients such as hedge funds, not retail clients, and it provides services rather than selling a narrow set of stocks.

rw: Segregating customer funds keeps them out of the firm's creditors' reach, so if the brokerage fails the customers' assets can be returned, which is the reason for the rule.

ww.To let the broker lend customer money to: Rules prohibit brokers from freely lending customers' money to others without consent, so separation does not exist to enable such lending; it exists to prevent misuse.
ww.To let the broker spend client money on: Spending client money on the firm's own costs would be misappropriation, which the segregation rule is meant to prevent, so it cannot be the rule's purpose.
ww.To lower the broker's taxes by showing l: Segregation has nothing to do with tax avoidance, and income reporting is not changed by holding customer money apart, so this reason is wrong.

rw: Front-running is a prohibited practice in which a broker trades for its own benefit ahead of a client's large order, expecting the order to move the price.

ww.A client who places a market order at th: A client placing a market order at the open is simply trading, and no one is trading ahead of anyone else's order, so it is not front-running.
ww.A broker running to the front of the tra: Front-running has nothing to do with a physical dash on the exchange floor; it is about using advance knowledge of a client order, not about timing before the bell.
ww.A broker who gives a client priority ove: Giving a client priority over others when orders are equal is fair handling or preferential treatment, whereas front-running means trading ahead of the client for the broker's profit.

rw: The Bank Secrecy Act requires institutions to file reports on large cash transactions and suspicious activity, to help authorities detect money laundering and other financial crimes.

ww.Banks to keep all customer information s: The Bank Secrecy Act requires banks to report certain information to the government, so it does the opposite of keeping all customer information secret from authorities.
ww.Banks to lend money to any customer who: The Act is an anti-money-laundering law and does not require banks to lend to any customer who asks, at the lowest rate available.
ww.Banks to publish the balance of each cus: Publishing customer balances publicly would violate privacy, and the Act does not require it; it requires reports to regulators and not publication to everyone.

rw: Transfer agents and registrars keep the shareholder list and track shares issued, preventing over-issuance and errors, so ownership records stay accurate for the company.

ww.To audit the financial statements of the: Auditing financial statements is done by independent auditors, not by a transfer agent or registrar, whose role is to keep records of owners and share issuance.
ww.To set the price at which shares will tr: Share prices are set by supply and demand in the market, not by a transfer agent or registrar, whose work is record keeping and not price setting.
ww.To decide how much dividend is paid to t: The board of directors decides dividend amounts, and a transfer agent may only help distribute them, so deciding the payment is not why companies use one.

rw: In a variable annuity, the value and payments change with the performance of underlying investment subaccounts, such as stock and bond funds, so the value is not fixed.

ww.An annuity that pays out its entire valu: Annuities are designed to pay out over time, often over a lifetime, so paying the entire value on the day of purchase is not how an annuity works.
ww.An annuity that pays a fixed, guaranteed: A fixed annuity, not a variable one, pays a guaranteed amount; a variable annuity's payments move with its investments and so can rise or fall with markets.
ww.An annuity that can be bought only by em: Variable annuities are sold to the general public by insurance companies and are not limited to employees of a large company, so this restriction is invented.

rw: An MLP is a partnership whose units trade on an exchange like stock, often in energy and pipelines, and it passes income through to investors for tax purposes.

ww.A government program that insures partne: An MLP is a traded business entity and not a government insurance program; insurance for partnerships against office losses is a different product altogether.
ww.A private agreement between two friends: A private agreement between two friends sharing shop profits is an ordinary general partnership, whereas an MLP is a large partnership with units that trade publicly.
ww.A bank account held jointly by two peopl: A joint bank account is a deposit product for two holders and is unrelated to an MLP, which is a publicly traded partnership.

rw: A DRIP automatically uses cash dividends to buy additional shares, often with no commission, which compounds the holding over time without the investor placing orders.

ww.A plan that sells the investor's shares: A DRIP does not sell shares when a dividend is due; it uses the dividend to buy more shares, so it adds to the position and does not sell.
ww.A plan that sends every dividend to a ch: A DRIP lets the shareholder choose to reinvest; dividends are not forced to go to a charity picked by the board, so that description is wrong.
ww.A plan that stops all dividends and repa: A DRIP does not stop dividends or repay bondholders; dividends continue and are simply reinvested, so this describes something unrelated to the plan.

rw: Emerging-market funds invest in developing economies, which can grow quickly but carry higher risks such as political instability and currency swings, which fits this description.

ww.A fund that is guaranteed to rise in val: No fund can be guaranteed to rise, because developing economies face political, currency, and economic risks, so the claim that growth is always assured is false.
ww.A fund that invests only in the oldest a: Funds holding only the oldest, most stable firms of rich countries describe a developed-market blue-chip fund, which is the opposite of an emerging-market fund.
ww.A fund that invests only in short-term g: Short-term home-country government debt describes a money market or Treasury bill fund, which is a safe domestic holding and not an emerging-market investment.

rw: Sector rotation shifts money among industries expected to do better at each stage of the economic cycle, such as moving to defensive sectors when growth slows.

ww.Holding the same industry for the whole: Holding the same industry forever with no change is a buy-and-hold concentration, which is the opposite of rotating among sectors as the cycle changes.
ww.Moving the investor's money between bank: Moving money between banks for the best cash rate is rate shopping for savings, which involves no stock sectors, so it is not sector rotation.
ww.Selling all stocks at the end of each ye: Selling every stock at year end and rebuying on the first day is a calendar trading idea, not sector rotation, which moves between industries.

rw: On the ex-dividend date, a buyer of the stock no longer gets the declared dividend, which goes to the previous owner, so it is the first day that happens.

ww.The day the board of directors votes on: The board vote that declares a dividend is the declaration date, not the ex-dividend date, and a declared dividend is rarely cut after that point.
ww.The day the dividend payment is actually: Payment of the dividend to eligible shareholders happens on the payable date, which comes after the ex-dividend date, so this describes a different event.
ww.The day the company announces that it wi: Announcing that the company will pay a dividend is the declaration date, which comes before the ex-dividend date, so this answer names the wrong event.

rw: The record date is when the company checks its books; only holders registered on that date receive the dividend, which is why it matters to shareholders.

ww.The date on which the company first anno: The first public announcement of a dividend happens on the declaration date, which comes before the record date and is a separate step in the sequence.
ww.The date on which the dividend is actual: The cash payout to eligible shareholders is the payable date, which happens after the record date, so this defines a different date in the dividend timeline.
ww.The date on which the stock first begins: Trading without the right to the next dividend begins on the ex-dividend date, which comes just before the record date, so this describes the wrong date.

rw: The stock typically drops by about the dividend amount on the ex-dividend date, so $40 minus the $1 dividend gives roughly $39, other things equal.

ww.About $40: The price should drop by about the dividend because the buyer no longer receives it, so opening near $40 would ignore that adjustment of about $1.
ww.About $1: The $1 figure is the dividend itself and not the stock price; the price stays near $40 less the dividend, so about $1 would be a drop of nearly all value.
ww.About $41: A price of $41 would add the dividend to the price, but the dividend leaves the stock on that date, so the price should fall, not rise.

rw: A stock dividend pays holders extra shares in proportion to their holdings, while a cash dividend pays money, so the difference is the form of payment.

ww.Shareholders receive cash and give up th: A stock dividend gives shares and not cash, and the holder keeps the original shares and does not give them up, so this description is incorrect.
ww.Shareholders must pay the company for ex: Stock dividends are distributed for free to existing shareholders, who do not pay the company anything for them, so a payment requirement is not part of it.
ww.Shareholders receive bonds in place of t: A stock dividend pays in additional shares of the company, not in bonds, so substituting bonds for cash is not how the dividend works.

rw: Cumulative preferred stock lets unpaid dividends accumulate as arrears, and the issuer must pay them in full before it can pay any common stock dividends.

ww.Preferred stock that gives the holder ex: Extra votes describe a voting preference feature and not cumulative dividends; the cumulative feature concerns unpaid dividends that accumulate and are owed before common holders are paid.
ww.Preferred stock that pays no dividends a: Cumulative preferred stock does pay dividends, and its defining feature is that missed ones build up, so saying it pays none is incorrect.
ww.Preferred stock that can be converted in: Conversion into bonds at the issuer's option is not what cumulative means; conversion features involve common shares, and cumulative concerns missed dividends.

rw: Convertible preferred stock may be exchanged by its holder for a set number of common shares, so the holder can benefit if the common price rises.

ww.Preferred stock that must be repaid in c: Repayment in cash on a fixed date describes a redeemable or maturing security, whereas convertible preferred gives the holder the right to exchange it for common shares.
ww.Preferred stock that can be sold only to: Convertible preferred is not limited to employees of the issuer and can be bought by ordinary investors, so a restriction to employees is not the definition.
ww.Preferred stock that can be converted in: Preferred stock converts into common stock of the issuer, not into a bank savings account, and banks are not involved in the conversion at all.

rw: Par value is a nominal figure stated in the corporate charter, often tiny, and it has little connection to what the stock trades for in the market.

ww.The price at which the stock currently t: The price at which stock currently trades is its market price, which changes every day, whereas par value is a fixed nominal amount set by the charter.
ww.The amount the company expects to earn o: Expected earnings per share are a profit measure and are unrelated to par value, which is a nominal legal figure and not a forecast of profit.
ww.The price investors paid in the initial: The price paid at the initial public offering is the offering price, which is set by market demand, not by the charter, so it is different from par value.

rw: TIPS are Treasury securities whose principal adjusts upward with inflation, as measured by the CPI, and so protect the investor's purchasing power.

ww.A Treasury bond with a fixed rate and no: A fixed-rate Treasury bond with no inflation adjustment is an ordinary Treasury note or bond, not a TIPS, whose principal changes with inflation.
ww.A corporate bond that pays more when inf: TIPS are issued by the U.S. Treasury, not corporations, and they pay more when inflation rises, not when it falls, so this reverses the facts.
ww.A municipal bond whose interest is taxed: TIPS are federal Treasury securities, not municipal bonds, and their interest is not taxed twice by a state, so this describes something else.

rw: Series EE bonds are U.S. savings bonds sold by the Treasury that earn interest over time, and the holder collects it when redeeming them.

ww.A bond sold by a private company to rais: A bond sold by a private company to fund a factory is a corporate bond, whereas a Series EE is a savings bond issued by the Treasury.
ww.A bond that lets the holder buy stock at: A bond letting the holder buy stock at a set price describes a bond with warrants or a convertible, not a Series EE savings bond.
ww.A bond that can be traded on a stock exc: Series EE savings bonds are not traded on exchanges at daily prices; they are bought from and redeemed through the Treasury, so this describes marketable bonds.

rw: A bond ladder spreads maturities across different dates so that bonds come due at regular intervals, which reduces reinvestment and interest rate risk.

ww.Buying many bonds that all mature on one: Buying bonds that all mature on one day is a bunched maturity and gives no staggered schedule, so it is not a ladder, which spreads maturities over time.
ww.Buying bonds only from the one top-rate: Buying from only one top issuer concentrates credit risk and says nothing about maturity dates, so it does not describe a bond ladder.
ww.Buying a bond and selling it the next da: Buying a bond and selling it the next day is short-term trading and has no maturity structure, so it is not a ladder.

rw: A CD ladder splits money among CDs with different maturity dates so that one matures regularly, giving access to cash and chances to capture higher rates.

ww.Putting money in a CD at one bank, then: Opening a CD at one bank and then another each month is bank hopping and does not set differing maturity dates for a planned schedule, so it is not a ladder.
ww.Putting all money into one CD that matur: Putting everything into one ten-year CD gives a single maturity, whereas a ladder uses several CDs maturing at different times to keep some money available.
ww.Buying stock using a CD as the only form: Using a CD as the only payment for stock purchases is not a ladder; a ladder is a way of timing CD maturities and does not involve buying stock.

rw: A thirty-year bond has the longest time to maturity, so a rise in interest rates cuts the present value of its distant payments the most.

ww.A 1-year bond: A one-year bond has a short life, so its price changes only modestly when rates rise; it is less sensitive than a thirty-year bond.
ww.A 3-month T-bill: A three-month T-bill matures almost immediately, so rate changes barely affect its price, making it far less rate sensitive than a long-term bond.
ww.A bond due today: A bond due today pays face value at once, so its price cannot change with rates, making it the least rate sensitive of all.

rw: Current yield is the annual interest payment divided by the bond's current market price, which shows the income return an investor gets for the price paid today.

ww.The bond's price divided by its yearly i: Dividing the price by the interest payment flips the ratio; current yield is the interest divided by the price, so this formula is upside down.
ww.The total return if held until it mature: The total return if held to maturity including coupons describes yield to maturity, which is a broader measure than current yield, which looks only at income.
ww.Annual interest divided by the bond's fa: Interest divided by face value at issue is the coupon rate, which does not change with the market price, so it is not the current yield.

rw: A premium bond trades above its face value, usually because its coupon exceeds current market rates, so investors pay more than par to own it.

ww.A bond trading below its face value: A bond trading below face value is a discount bond, not a premium bond, and it typically has a coupon below current market rates.
ww.A bond trading exactly at face value: A bond trading exactly at face value is said to trade at par, which is different from a premium bond, which is above par.
ww.A bond that pays no interest at all: A bond that pays no interest at all is a zero-coupon bond, which usually trades at a deep discount, not a premium.

rw: The bond trades at $1,050, which is $50 above its $1,000 face value, so it is trading at a premium.

ww.Trading right at par: Par means the bond trades at its $1,000 face value, but at $1,050 the price is above par, so it is not described that way.
ww.Trading at maturity: Maturity is when the bond's principal is repaid, not a description of its trading price, so trading at maturity does not describe a $1,050 price.
ww.Trading at a discount: A discount would mean a price below the $1,000 face value, but $1,050 is above it, so it cannot be described as a discount.

rw: A GO bond is a municipal bond backed by the issuer's full faith and credit and its power to tax, which supports repayment.

ww.A federal bond backed by the U.S. Treasu: A federal bond backed by the Treasury is a Treasury security, not a general obligation bond, which is issued by a state or local government.
ww.A municipal bond backed only by revenue: A bond backed only by revenue from one project is a revenue bond, whereas a general obligation bond is backed by the issuer's full taxing power.
ww.A corporate bond backed by the assets of: A bond backed by a factory's assets is a corporate secured bond, not a municipal GO bond, which relies on taxing power and not on specific assets.

rw: A revenue bond is a municipal bond repaid from the income of a specific project, such as tolls from a road, rather than from general taxes.

ww.A bond repaid from the issuer's general: A bond repaid from general tax receipts such as property taxes is a general obligation bond, which differs from a revenue bond, repaid from project income.
ww.A bond that matures in under one year an: A bond that matures within one year and pays no interest until redeemed describes a short-term discount instrument and not a revenue bond, which is a longer-term municipal debt.
ww.A bond that gives the holder a share of: A revenue bond is not an equity share; it does not give the holder a share of a company's revenue or a vote at meetings.

rw: Municipal bond interest is often exempt from federal income tax, which is worth the most to investors in high tax brackets who would otherwise pay more tax.

ww.The bond never loses value, whatever hap: Municipal bonds can lose value when rates rise or an issuer's credit weakens, so the claim that they never lose value whatever happens is false.
ww.The bond is guaranteed by the federal go: Municipal bonds are issued by states and local governments, not guaranteed by the federal government, so this claim is incorrect and unrelated to their tax benefit.
ww.Interest is always taxed more than other: Being taxed more than other bonds would be a drawback and no reason to prefer them; municipal interest is often exempt, not taxed more.

rw: The equivalent taxable yield is 3 divided by (1 minus 0.25), or 3 divided by 0.75, which equals 4 percent, so a taxable bond must pay 4 percent to match.

ww.28 percent: Adding the 25 percent bracket to 3 percent to get 28 percent is arithmetic nonsense; the correct method is dividing 3 by one minus 0.25, not adding.
ww.2.25 percent: Multiplying 3 percent by 0.75 gives 2.25 percent, which is the after-tax yield of a taxable bond, not the taxable yield needed to equal 3 percent tax-free.
ww.3 percent: A 3 percent taxable yield would be reduced by tax to 2.25 percent after tax, which is below the 3 percent tax-free yield, so it is not equivalent.

rw: A covered call means selling a call option on shares you already own, which earns the premium and covers the obligation to deliver those shares.

ww.Selling a call option without owning the: Selling a call option without owning the stock is a naked call, which is risky; a covered call requires that the seller already owns the shares.
ww.Buying a call option without owning the: Buying a call option without owning the stock is a long call, which is a bullish purchase, whereas a covered call involves selling a call.
ww.Buying a put option on stock you own to: Buying a put option on stock you own is a protective put, which limits downside, whereas a covered call sells a call to earn income.

rw: A protective put buys a put on stock you own, so if the price falls you can sell at the strike, which limits the downside.

ww.Buying a call option to bet on a rise in: Buying a call to bet on a price rise is a long call, a bullish speculation, whereas a protective put guards an owned position against a fall.
ww.Selling a stock short to profit if its p: Selling a stock short profits if the price falls, but it is a separate strategy and not a put purchase protecting shares you own.
ww.Selling a put option on a stock you own,: Selling a put on stock you own earns a premium but adds an obligation to buy more, and it does not protect the shares from falling.

rw: The call is worth $70 minus $60, or $10, at expiration; subtracting the $4 premium paid leaves a net profit of $6 per share.

ww.$10: The stock finishes $10 above the $60 strike, but the $4 premium paid must be subtracted, so $10 is the gross value, not the net profit.
ww.$4: The $4 figure is only the premium paid, a cost of the position, so it is not the profit; the option's $10 value less $4 gives $6.
ww.$14: Adding the $4 premium to the $10 intrinsic value gives $14, but premium paid is a cost that is subtracted, so net profit is $6 and not $14.

rw: With the stock at $52, above the $50 strike, the put is out of the money and expires worthless, so the buyer loses the $2 premium.

ww.A loss of $52: A loss of $52 would be the stock's price, but the put buyer's maximum loss is only the $2 premium paid, so this is incorrect.
ww.A gain of $52: A gain of $52 would imply the stock's whole price was profit, which cannot happen; the put expires worthless at $52 against a $50 strike, losing the premium.
ww.A gain of $2: A gain of $2 would require the put to finish in the money, but at $52 above the $50 strike it expires worthless and the $2 premium is lost.

rw: A call's intrinsic value is the stock price minus the strike, so $48 minus $40 equals $8 per share, the amount it is in the money.

ww.$40: The $40 figure is only the strike price; intrinsic value is the stock price minus the strike, not the strike itself, which would be $48 minus $40.
ww.$48: The $48 figure is the stock price; intrinsic value subtracts the $40 strike from it, so $48 is not the option's intrinsic value.
ww.$88: Adding the stock price and strike to get $88 is wrong; intrinsic value is found by subtracting the strike from the stock price, which gives $8.

rw: As expiration approaches, there is less time for the underlying price to move favorably, so the time value portion of an option's price declines toward zero.

ww.Its time value rises: Time value does not rise as expiration nears, because less time remains for the price to move favorably, so the option's chance of gaining falls.
ww.Its time value is steady: Time value does not hold steady; it erodes as expiration approaches, and the erosion tends to speed up in the final weeks, so it is not constant.
ww.Its time value doubles: Time value cannot double as expiration nears; with less time left there is less chance of a favorable move, so it shrinks and does not grow.

rw: The ex-rights date determines who is entitled to a rights offering, because buyers on or after that date no longer receive the rights, like the ex-dividend date.

ww.Choosing the exchange for a stock listin: Choosing the exchange where a firm lists its stock is a listing decision made by the company, unrelated to the ex-rights date, which concerns rights offerings.
ww.Setting the interest rate on a corporate: A corporate bond's interest rate is set at issuance by the issuer and market conditions, and has nothing to do with a stock's ex-rights date.
ww.Setting the dividend yield for the next: The dividend yield depends on the dividend and the price and is not set by the ex-rights date, which concerns eligibility for a rights offering.

rw: A lock-up bars insiders and early investors from selling their shares for a set time after the IPO, which prevents a flood of sales that could drop the price.

ww.A time when the exchange is closed for t: The exchange stays open for trading after a listing; a lock-up restricts specific holders' sales and does not close the exchange to new listings.
ww.A time when the public cannot buy shares: The public can buy shares once the IPO trades; the lock-up limits insiders' sales and does not stop the public from buying, so this is reversed.
ww.A time when the company cannot pay any d: A lock-up concerns sales by insiders, not dividends; the company is not barred from paying dividends because of the lock-up, so this is a different matter.

rw: In a quiet period, the company and its underwriters limit promotional statements before and after the IPO so investors rely on the prospectus and not on hype.

ww.A time when the stock market is closed f: A quiet period concerns the company's communications around an IPO, not market holidays or weekend closures, which are routine schedule events unrelated to securities offerings.
ww.A time when the company stops operating: A company does not shut down operations in a quiet period; it continues to operate normally, while limits apply only to its promotional statements.
ww.A time when trading volume is at its low: A quiet period is a regulatory limit on promotion, not a low-volume stretch around year end, so describing a seasonal trading lull misses its meaning.

rw: A SPAC is a shell company that raises money in an IPO and then uses it to acquire a private company, taking that company public.

ww.A bond issued by a state government to b: A bond issued by a state to build roads and schools is a municipal bond, whereas a SPAC is a shell company that raises money through an IPO.
ww.A savings plan for retirement offered by: A work retirement savings plan offered by employers is a 401(k) or similar, not a SPAC, which is a company formed to buy a business.
ww.A fund that invests in stocks of space a: A fund investing in space and rocket firms would be a thematic fund; the name resembles the word space, but a SPAC is a special purpose acquisition company.

rw: Float is the number of shares available for the public to trade, which excludes shares held by insiders and restricted holders, so it measures tradable supply.

ww.The total amount of money a company has: The money a company holds in the bank is its cash balance, a balance sheet item, and it does not measure the shares available for public trading.
ww.The number of shares the company has bou: Shares the company has bought back are treasury shares, which are removed from the float, so this describes something different from the float.
ww.The price at which shares are first offe: The price at which shares are first offered is the IPO or offering price, which is unrelated to how many shares are available for trading.

rw: Short interest is the total number of shares that investors have sold short and have not yet covered, which indicates bearish sentiment and potential for a squeeze.

ww.The commission a broker charges for a sh: Commissions on short trades are a broker's charge for the transaction, whereas short interest counts the shares sold short that have not been covered or closed out.
ww.The interest paid on a short-term bond o: Interest paid on a short-term bond or note is a bond yield, whereas short interest refers to shares sold short and not to any interest payment.
ww.The interest a bank pays on a savings ac: Interest a bank pays on savings is a deposit return, which is unrelated to short selling; short interest counts open short positions in a stock.

rw: In a short squeeze, a rising price forces short sellers to buy shares to cover their losses, and that buying pushes the price higher still.

ww.A tax charged to short sellers on the pr: A short squeeze is a market event and not a tax; short sellers' profits are taxed under ordinary rules, and no special tax is named a squeeze.
ww.A rule that stops short selling when a s: A rule that restricts short selling after a ten percent daily fall is the alternative uptick rule, which differs from a short squeeze, a price spike.
ww.A fall in price that forces buyers to se: A fall in price forcing buyers to sell is a long squeeze or panic selling, the reverse of a short squeeze, where rising prices force shorts to buy.

rw: An American option can be exercised at any time up to and including expiration, which gives the holder more flexibility than a European option.

ww.An option that is sold only to U.S. citi: American options are not restricted to U.S. citizens; the term describes when the option can be exercised, not who may buy it, so the description is wrong.
ww.An option on a U.S. stock only and not o: The label American refers to the exercise style, not the underlying market, and such options can exist on foreign stocks too, so it is not limited to U.S. stocks.
ww.An option that can be exercised only on: An option exercisable only on the expiration date is a European option, which is the opposite of the American style that allows earlier exercise.

rw: A stop-limit order turns into a limit order once the stop price is reached, so it fills only at the limit price or better, which controls the price.

ww.An order that executes at any price once: An order that executes at any price once a stop is reached is a stop order, which becomes a market order and offers no price limit.
ww.An order to buy a set number of shares o: An order to buy a set number of shares on a fixed day each month is a recurring purchase plan, not a stop-limit order, which depends on price.
ww.An order that is canceled when the marke: Cancellation at the market open describes no standard stop-limit feature; a stop-limit order remains until triggered, filled, or canceled by its time terms, whatever the open.

rw: A good-til-canceled order stays active until it is filled or the investor cancels it, though brokers often set a maximum duration such as 60 or 90 days.

ww.An order that must be filled immediately: An order that must be filled immediately or canceled in full is a fill-or-kill order, not a GTC order, which remains open for a longer time.
ww.An order that is canceled when the price: A GTC order is not canceled by small price changes; it remains active until filled or canceled, so a minor price move does not end it.
ww.An order that expires at the end of the: An order that expires at the end of the trading day is a day order, which is the default, whereas a GTC order lasts longer.

rw: An all-or-none order must be executed in its entirety or not at all, so partial fills are not allowed, which can delay or prevent execution.

ww.An order that is filled in parts at any: An order filled in parts at any price describes a partial fill with no price condition, whereas an AON order requires the full quantity or nothing.
ww.An order that trades all stocks in an in: Trading all stocks in an index at once describes a basket or program trade, not an AON order, which is about filling the whole quantity.
ww.An order that applies to all of an inves: An AON order applies to a single order's quantity and does not cover all of an investor's accounts, so this description is incorrect.

rw: A margin account lets an investor borrow money from the broker to buy securities, using the account's holdings as collateral for the loan.

ww.A savings account: A savings account is a bank deposit account and gives no borrowing power to buy securities; borrowing from a broker requires a margin account.
ww.A traditional IRA: A traditional IRA is a retirement account that generally cannot be used for margin borrowing, so it does not let an investor borrow from a broker to buy securities.
ww.A cash account: A cash account requires securities to be paid for in full and does not allow borrowing, so it is the opposite of an account for borrowing.

rw: In a cash account, securities must be paid for in full, with no borrowing from the broker, which limits risk to the funds deposited.

ww.An account that lets the investor borrow: A cash account does not let the investor borrow; borrowing without limits is not allowed in any brokerage account, and margin accounts have limits too.
ww.An account that holds only paper cash in: A cash account is a brokerage account and does not mean physical bills stored in a vault; the cash is recorded electronically in the account.
ww.An account that pays higher interest tha: Brokerage cash accounts do not guarantee higher interest than banks; the name refers to full payment for trades, not to the interest rate earned.

rw: A joint brokerage account is owned by two or more people, who share rights to the assets, as with spouses or family members.

ww.An account that only children can use: A joint brokerage account is owned by two or more adults, not only children; children's accounts are custodial accounts, which differ from joint accounts.
ww.An account owned by a brokerage and a ba: A brokerage and a bank do not co-own a joint account; joint ownership refers to two or more individual customers, not to institutions.
ww.An account shared by a firm and customer: A firm and its customers do not share a joint account; joint means two or more individuals co-owning the account, so this description is wrong.

rw: A rollover IRA receives funds moved from an employer plan such as a 401(k), which lets the saver keep the tax-deferred status of retirement savings.

ww.An IRA that pays out its balance on the: A rollover IRA holds funds moved from another retirement plan and does not pay out its balance on the first day it is opened.
ww.An IRA that rolls into a savings account: A rollover IRA stays invested in retirement holdings and does not roll into a savings account each year at a fixed rate, so this is invented.
ww.An IRA that can be opened only by retire: A rollover IRA can be opened by workers of any age who leave a job, not only retirees over age 65, so that restriction is false.

rw: A SEP IRA is a simplified employee pension plan that lets self-employed people and small business owners save for retirement, with relatively high contribution limits.

ww.A plan that pays a fixed income to retir: A plan paying fixed income for life describes an annuity or pension; a SEP IRA is a retirement savings plan funded by contributions, not a payout promise.
ww.A savings plan for students saving for c: A savings plan for college with tuition tax breaks is a 529 plan, whereas a SEP IRA is for retirement savings.
ww.A plan that is available only to large c: A SEP IRA is designed for small businesses and the self-employed, being simple to run, so claiming it is only for large corporations is false.

rw: Class A shares carry a front-end sales charge but usually have lower annual fees than other classes, which suits long-term holders who pay the load up front.

ww.A share that pays no dividends and has n: Class A shares are ordinary fund shares that pay dividends and carry voting rights, so claiming they pay none and have no vote is wrong.
ww.A share with no sales charge and the hig: No sales charge with the highest annual fees describes Class C shares more closely, whereas Class A has a front-end load and lower ongoing fees.
ww.A share that can be bought only by emplo: Class A shares are sold to the general public, not only to employees of the fund company, so the restriction in this answer is invented.

rw: A back-end load is a sales charge paid when fund shares are sold, often declining the longer the shares are held.

ww.A sales charge paid when fund shares are: A sales charge paid when fund shares are bought is a front-end load, the opposite of a back-end load, which is charged at the time of sale.
ww.A fee for transferring an account to ano: A fee for transferring an account to another firm is an account transfer or closing fee, which is separate from a back-end sales load on selling shares.
ww.An annual fee for marketing the fund to: An annual fee for marketing the fund is a 12b-1 fee, which is charged yearly and is different from a back-end load, charged once on sale.

rw: A no-load fund charges no sales commission to buy or sell shares, though it still has annual operating expenses, so more of the investment goes to work.

ww.A fund that charges no fees of any kind,: No-load funds avoid sales commissions but still charge annual expenses such as management fees, so the claim of no fees of any kind is false.
ww.A fund that holds no securities of any k: A no-load fund holds securities like any other fund; the term refers to sales charges, not to holding no securities and only cash.
ww.A fund that is not regulated by the SEC: No-load funds are regulated by the SEC like other mutual funds, so the claim that no agency regulates them is false.

rw: A money market fund invests in cash equivalents and short-term debt such as Treasury bills and commercial paper, so it matches the description most closely.

ww.An emerging-market fund: An emerging-market fund invests in stocks and sometimes bonds of developing economies, which carry more risk and are not primarily cash equivalents.
ww.A small-cap stock fund: A small-cap stock fund holds equities of small companies, so it is not built around cash equivalents or short-term debt.
ww.A sector stock fund: A sector stock fund concentrates in the stocks of one industry, so it holds equities and not primarily cash equivalents or short-term debt.

rw: Smart-beta ETFs follow rules-based factors such as value, momentum, or low volatility instead of weighting holdings purely by market capitalization, which is their defining trait.

ww.An ETF that is guaranteed to beat the ma: No ETF can be guaranteed to beat the market every year, and smart-beta funds still carry the risk that factor strategies lag, so that claim is false.
ww.An ETF that picks stocks by a manager's: Smart-beta ETFs follow published, rules-based methods, so an ETF using gut feeling with no rules and no published method is the opposite of smart beta.
ww.An ETF that holds only cash and short-te: An ETF holding only cash and short-term notes would be a money market or ultra short-term fund, not a smart-beta equity fund.

rw: An inverse ETF is designed to gain when the index it tracks falls, usually using derivatives, which lets investors profit from or hedge against declines.

ww.An ETF that holds only bonds and pays in: An ETF holding bonds and paying interest monthly is a bond ETF, which rises and falls with the bond market and not against an index.
ww.An ETF that pays no dividends and tracks: Paying no dividends and tracking small companies describes a small-cap growth fund, not an inverse ETF, whose defining trait is moving opposite to its index.
ww.An ETF designed to rise whenever the ind: An ETF designed to rise when its index rises is an ordinary index ETF, whereas an inverse ETF is built to move the other way.

rw: A leveraged ETF uses borrowing or derivatives to seek a multiple of its index's daily return, such as two or three times, which magnifies both gains and losses.

ww.An ETF that guarantees a gain each year: No ETF can guarantee yearly gains; leveraged ETFs magnify losses as well as gains, so a guaranteed gain regardless of the index is false.
ww.An ETF that holds only government bonds: An ETF holding very short-maturity government bonds is a low-risk bond fund and uses no leverage, so it does not match the leveraged ETF definition.
ww.An ETF that tracks an index one-for-one: An ETF that tracks its index one-for-one without borrowing is a standard index ETF, which is the opposite of a leveraged ETF.

rw: A commodity ETF tracks the price of a commodity such as gold or oil, giving investors exposure without owning the physical goods or futures contracts directly.

ww.An ETF that holds shares in grocery stor: A commodity ETF tracks commodity prices and not grocery store shares, so holding only grocery stocks and no commodities describes a retail stock fund instead.
ww.An ETF that guarantees stable prices for: No fund can guarantee stable prices for commodities, which are volatile, so a commodity ETF reflects commodity price swings and not stability.
ww.An ETF that is available only to farmers: Commodity ETFs trade on exchanges and are open to ordinary investors, not only farmers and grain producers, so this restriction is invented.

rw: A bond ETF holds a basket of bonds and trades on an exchange like a stock, giving investors diversified bond exposure with intraday trading.

ww.An ETF that pays no interest and holds o: A bond ETF holds bonds that pay interest, which flows to shareholders, so describing one as paying no interest and holding only cash is wrong.
ww.An ETF that holds only stocks of large c: An ETF holding only large company stocks is an equity ETF, so it does not match a bond ETF, which holds bonds.
ww.An ETF that matures on a fixed date like: A bond ETF is a fund with no single fixed maturity date and does not repay holders on a set day like one bond, so it differs.

rw: ESG funds consider environmental, social, and governance factors when choosing investments, which lets investors align their holdings with values as well as returns.

ww.A fund that guarantees higher returns th: No fund can guarantee higher returns than the market in every year, and ESG funds can lag, so a guarantee of outperformance is false.
ww.A fund that is run by a government agenc: ESG funds are offered by private asset managers to the general public, not run by a state agency for public employees only, so this is incorrect.
ww.A fund that invests only in energy compa: An ESG fund screens by environmental, social, and governance factors across industries, so it is not limited to energy companies, and it often avoids some fossil fuel firms.

rw: A dividend aristocrat is a company in the S&P 500 that has raised its dividend every year for at least 25 years, showing reliable payouts.

ww.A company owned by a royal family and ru: A dividend aristocrat is defined by a record of dividend increases, not by royal ownership or family heirs, so this description does not match the term.
ww.A company that has never paid a dividend: A company that has never paid a dividend cannot be a dividend aristocrat, which requires a long record of paying and raising dividends.
ww.A company that pays dividends in gold ba: Paying dividends in gold bars is not a feature of dividend aristocrats, which pay cash dividends; the term refers to years of increases.

rw: A defensive stock tends to hold up when the economy weakens, because demand for products like utilities and food stays steady, so earnings are more stable.

ww.A stock that rises fastest in booms and: A stock rising fastest in booms and falling hardest in downturns is a cyclical or high-beta stock, which is the opposite of a defensive stock.
ww.A stock that has no risk at all, because: No stock has zero risk, and a firm can lose money in a year, so describing a defensive stock as riskless is false.
ww.A stock of a company that makes weapons: Defensive stocks are defined by resilience in downturns and not by selling weapons; a weapons maker is only one example and is not the meaning of the term.

rw: A cyclical stock's performance rises and falls with the business cycle, doing well in expansions and poorly in recessions, as with autos, travel, and construction firms.

ww.A stock that is unaffected by the econom: A stock unaffected by the economy in good times or bad describes a defensive stock, so it is the opposite of a cyclical stock.
ww.A stock traded only in yearly cycles, ri: Cyclical refers to the business cycle and not to yearly seasons; there is no rule that such stocks rise in spring and fall later.
ww.A stock that pays no dividends and never: Cyclical stocks can pay dividends and their prices change often, so a stock that never changes in price and pays no dividends is not cyclical.

rw: An upward-sloping yield curve means that bonds with longer maturities pay higher yields than shorter ones, the usual pattern as investors want extra pay for longer lending.

ww.All bonds yield the same rate, whatever: If all bonds yielded the same rate regardless of term, the yield curve would be flat and not upward sloping, so this does not describe it.
ww.Bonds pay no interest, so yields are all: Bonds pay interest and yields are not all zero in a normal market, and a sloping curve shows yields that differ by maturity, so this is incorrect.
ww.Shorter-term bonds yield more than longe: Shorter-term bonds yielding more than longer-term ones describes an inverted curve, which slopes downward and is the opposite of an upward slope.

rw: A flat yield curve shows little difference between short and long rates, which often appears at a turning point in the economic cycle, as growth changes.

ww.Long-term rates far above short-term rat: Long-term rates far above short-term rates describe a steep upward-sloping curve, so it is not a flat curve, whose short and long yields are close.
ww.Bonds are about to mature and all will b: A flat yield curve says nothing about bonds about to mature and being repaid in days; it describes similar yields across maturities, so this is unrelated.
ww.Rates falling to zero across every matur: A flat curve means similar yields across maturities, not rates falling to zero; the level can be well above zero, so bonds still pay interest.

rw: The federal funds rate is the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserve balances, and the Federal Reserve targets it to guide monetary policy.

ww.The rate a bank charges a home buyer for: A mortgage rate is set by lenders for home loans and differs from the federal funds rate, which is an overnight interbank rate for reserves.
ww.The rate of inflation measured by prices: The rate of inflation over the past year is measured by indexes such as the CPI, not by the federal funds rate, which is an interest rate.
ww.The rate the government pays on its Trea: The rate the government pays on Treasury bonds is the Treasury yield, which is set by market auctions and differs from the overnight federal funds rate.

rw: In quantitative easing, a central bank buys securities such as government bonds, which adds money to the financial system and pushes long-term interest rates lower.

ww.A rule limiting bank loans to households: A rule limiting bank loans would be a regulation or credit control, whereas quantitative easing involves a central bank buying securities to add money to the economy.
ww.A way for firms to report profits to inv: Reporting profits to investors each quarter is financial reporting by firms, which has nothing to do with central bank policy or quantitative easing.
ww.A tax cut passed by the legislature to l: A tax cut passed by the legislature is fiscal policy, whereas quantitative easing is monetary policy carried out by the central bank.

rw: A correction is a decline of 10 percent or more from a recent high, usually smaller than a bear market, which is often defined as a 20 percent fall.

ww.A fall of 50 percent or more from a high: A fall of 50 percent or more from a high is a deep bear market or crash, which is much larger than a correction, defined as about 10 percent.
ww.A rise of 10 percent or more from a rece: A rise of 10 percent or more from a recent low is a rally, which goes up, whereas a correction is a decline.
ww.A change in a stock's ticker symbol afte: A change in a stock's ticker symbol after a merger is a symbol change and has nothing to do with price declines, which define a correction.

rw: A stock market crash is a sudden, steep fall in stock prices, often driven by panic selling, as in 1929 or 1987.

ww.A slow, steady rise in stock prices: A slow and steady rise in prices is a bull market or gradual gain, which is the opposite of a crash, defined by sudden steep falls.
ww.A closure of the exchange for a holiday: A closure of the exchange for a holiday is a scheduled market holiday, not a crash, which is about a sharp and rapid fall in prices.
ww.A computer failure at a brokerage: A computer failure at a brokerage is a technical outage that may affect trading but is not a crash, which refers to broad price declines.

rw: The Russell 2000 tracks about 2,000 small-cap U.S. stocks, so it is commonly used as a measure of small company performance in the market.

ww.An index of the 30 largest U.S. firms: An index of the 30 largest U.S. firms describes the Dow Jones Industrial Average, which has 30 stocks, not the Russell 2000 small-cap index.
ww.An index of 500 large companies: An index of 500 large companies describes the S&P 500, whose name states its count, whereas the Russell 2000 covers small companies.
ww.An index of foreign government bonds: The Russell 2000 is a stock index of small U.S. companies, not an index of foreign government bonds, which are fixed income and not equities.

rw: MSCI EAFE tracks stocks in developed markets in Europe, Australasia, and the Far East, which are outside North America, so it is a common international benchmark.

ww.An index of emerging-market bonds and no: MSCI EAFE tracks stocks and not emerging-market bonds; it covers developed markets in Europe, Australasia, and the Far East, so a bond index of emerging markets is wrong.
ww.An index of commodity prices for oil, me: An index of commodity prices for oil, metals, and grain is a commodity index, not MSCI EAFE, which measures developed-market stocks.
ww.An index of U.S. small-cap stocks that t: An index of U.S. small-cap stocks is the Russell 2000, while MSCI EAFE covers companies outside the United States and Canada.

rw: In a price-weighted index such as the Dow, a stock with a higher share price moves the index more than one with a lower price.

ww.An index in which all stocks have equal: An index where all stocks have equal weight regardless of price is equal weighted, not price weighted, which gives higher-priced stocks more influence.
ww.An index based on trading volume only an: An index based on trading volume only describes a volume-based measure, not a price-weighted index, where weights come from share prices.
ww.An index in which larger companies have: Larger companies having more influence by market value describes a market-cap-weighted index, not a price-weighted index, where share price determines weight.

rw: In a market-cap-weighted index such as the S&P 500, bigger companies by market value have more influence on the index's movements than smaller ones.

ww.An index in which all stocks have equal: An index in which all stocks have equal weight is equal weighted, so it does not give larger companies more influence as market-cap weighting does.
ww.An index in which higher-priced stocks h: Higher-priced stocks having more influence describes a price-weighted index like the Dow, not a market-cap-weighted index, which depends on company size.
ww.An index based on a company's age and ye: A company's age and years listed do not set weights in a market-cap-weighted index; weights come from the market value of outstanding shares.

rw: In an equal-weighted index each stock has the same weight, so small and large companies move the index equally, regardless of price or size.

ww.An index in which pricier stocks have mo: Giving pricier stocks more influence describes a price-weighted index, which differs from an equal-weighted index, where each stock counts the same.
ww.An index in which larger companies have: Larger companies having more influence describes a market-cap-weighted index, whereas an equal-weighted index treats every stock alike, regardless of size.
ww.An index made of only two large stocks o: An equal-weighted index has many stocks, not only two, and the number of holdings is unrelated to weighting, so this description is wrong.

rw: A benchmark, such as an index, is a standard for comparing a portfolio's performance, so investors can tell if a manager is adding value.

ww.A bonus paid to fund managers who beat t: A bonus paid to managers who beat the market is a performance fee, not a benchmark, which is a standard used for comparison.
ww.A bench in the broker's lobby where clie: A bench in the broker's lobby is a piece of furniture unrelated to investing; the word benchmark simply happens to contain the word bench.
ww.A tool for measuring the fees of a fund,: A tool for measuring fees run by the fund manager is not a benchmark; a benchmark is an external standard, such as an index, to compare returns.

rw: The fund earned 8 percent while its benchmark earned 10 percent, a shortfall of 2 percentage points, so it underperformed its benchmark.

ww.It had no risk at all in the year: Lower returns do not show that a fund had no risk; the comparison involves returns only, and a fund always carries some investment risk.
ww.It outperformed its benchmark: A fund returning 8 percent against a benchmark's 10 percent earned less, so saying it outperformed has the comparison backward.
ww.It matched its benchmark exactly: Matching exactly would require equal returns, but 8 percent and 10 percent differ by 2 percentage points, so the fund did not match its benchmark.

rw: In an efficient market, prices reflect all available information, so it is hard to find bargains or overpriced securities consistently.

ww.A market controlled by the government, w: In an efficient market, prices come from many investors reacting to information, not from a government that sets prices, so this describes a controlled market.
ww.A market with no fees or taxes of any ki: Efficiency is about how prices reflect information, not about the absence of fees and taxes, which most markets do charge, so this is incorrect.
ww.A market that is open 24 hours a day, ev: Operating hours do not define efficiency; a market open around the clock can still be inefficient, so this confuses availability with how information is reflected in prices.

rw: If prices reflect available information, consistently beating the market is difficult, because gains are mostly luck, risk, or costs, and not repeatable skill.

ww.It is easy to do with a simple tip: If prices already reflect available information, simple tips are already built into the price, so beating the market with one is not easy.
ww.It is guaranteed with research: The hypothesis says research cannot guarantee beating the market, since prices already reflect information, so claiming a guarantee contradicts the theory.
ww.It is illegal in most countries: Beating the market is legal in nearly all countries, and the efficient market hypothesis says it is hard, not illegal, so this confuses difficulty with prohibition.
